title: As one that serveth (Luke 22:24–27)
hook: at the supper they argue about greatness; he says I am among you as one that serves

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bread and the cup in the upper room. Your line was do this. Did you pause before a meal? Day four hundred eighty.

Here's a detail that's easy to skip, and almost painful once you see it. In Luke, the very next thing after the bread and the cup is an argument. Jesus has just said this is my body, given for you. He's just told them one of them will betray him. And the apostles, at that same table, start arguing about which of them is the greatest. It's so human it hurts. Like a family bickering over who gets the good chair at a hospital bedside. Only Luke puts this argument right here, at the Last Supper. Today, how Jesus answers it.
screen: `RIGHT AFTER THE BREAD AND CUP.` → `WHICH OF US IS THE GREATEST?` → `ONLY LUKE PUTS IT HERE.`

segments.voice: Luke says: "And there was also a strife amongst them, which of them should seem to be the greater." Jesus doesn't scold them for wanting to matter. He redraws what mattering means. The kings of the nations lord it over people, he says, and the people in power like to be called benefactors. "But you not so." Let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves. Then he asks a simple question about the room they're sitting in. Who's greater, the one reclining at table or the one serving? Obviously, the one at table. Everybody knows that. "But I am in the midst of you, as he that serveth." He doesn't say I'm like a servant. He says, I am in the midst of you as one serving. Present tense. Right now, at this table. The Greek word is diakonon, the one who waits on tables. It's the root of the word deacon. Catholics have taken this very seriously in how the Church is shaped. Every priest and bishop is first ordained a deacon, a servant, and that service is never supposed to wear off. And since Pope Gregory the Great, around the year 600, popes have used the title servant of the servants of God, servus servorum Dei, at the head of their official letters. The highest office in the Church calls itself by the lowest job at the table. That's not a reason to think any of them always lived up to it. It's the standard Jesus set, at the table, the night before he died: greatness is measured by who you serve.
screen: `A STRIFE ABOUT GREATNESS.` · `BUT YOU NOT SO.` · `DIAKONON: THE ONE WHO WAITS TABLES.` · `SERVANT OF THE SERVANTS OF GOD.` · then, large: `I AM IN THE MIDST OF YOU AS HE THAT SERVETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: serve without being asked. Settle, and breathe. Picture the rooms you'll be in today: home, work, a bus, a store. Where is there a small job nobody wants? Dishes in the sink, a full trash bag, a spill, a coworker drowning in a task, a parent who's tired. Choose one, and decide to just do it without announcing it or waiting to be thanked. Picture yourself doing it quietly. If you pray, offer it as service. The bell holds the time.
As one that serveth. Jesus' answer to his apostles' argument at the Last Supper: I am among you as the one who waits on the table. Today's word.
Your line: as one that serveth. Today, do one small job nobody asked you to do, and don't mention it. Day four hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Every Catholic priest and bishop is first ordained a deacon, and on Holy Thursday the priest washes the feet of members of the congregation in memory of Christ serving at the Last Supper.

original.note: Greek: the one serving, waiting on tables. The root of the word deacon.

trapdoor: what you thought: as one that serveth is a nice humble saying.
what it means: at his last meal, Jesus places himself in the lowest job at the table and makes that the measure of greatness.
what a scholar hears: diakonon, the one waiting tables; popes have signed as servus servorum Dei since Gregory the Great (590–604).

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 22:24, 22:26 ('But you not so') and 22:27.
The index carry 'as one that serveth' differs slightly from the Douay 'as he that serveth'; the carry is kept exactly as indexed and the voice quotes the Douay. Owner may wish to align the index.
Servus servorum Dei: used by Gregory the Great (pope 590–604) and by later popes in official documents. Confirm phrasing.
Luke places the dispute at the supper; Mark and Matthew place a similar dispute earlier. Confirm 'only Luke puts this argument right here'.
